primary_new_grammar.label: Passato prossimo (avere/essere + participle, agreement with essere) against the passato remoto; regular and irregular participles; indirect-object clitics gli, le; partitive ne

cover.alt: Night in the shuttered Cerchi shop: Lapo writes in the big account book while Ser Bindo stands at his shoulder.
cover.art_brief: Night, 1 May 1300, inside the Cerchi company shop at Porta San Piero, Florence. The street shutters and door are closed and barred. One small oil lamp on the long counter lights a large open account book. Lapo, a lean dark-haired boy of sixteen in a plain tunic, sits at the book with a quill; his writing hand is tense. Ser Bindo, an old thin clean-shaven bookkeeper in a dark long gown and close cap, stands beside him, one hand flat and steady on the open page. Bales of wool and folded cloth on shelves in shadow. Through a crack in the shutters, the faint glow of torches in the street. No other people. Ink outline and restrained watercolour wash. No text, lettering, numbers or captions anywhere, including on the book's pages.

inference_aids.alt: Evening in the piazza of Santa Trinita: two companies of young riders halt face to face while dancing women scatter; Lapo and Gherardo watch from the edge of the crowd.
inference_aids.art_brief: At this segment: evening of 1 May 1300, the small piazza in front of the church of Santa Trinita, Florence, with the Spini palace (a tall stone house-palace) at one side. Low warm light, long shadows. In the middle, two companies of young noblemen on horseback have just halted face to face, horse against horse: on the left the Donati company, on the right the Cerchi company, about five riders each, in bright fine woollen gowns and hoods, no armour; no sword is drawn yet, but one rider has his hand on the hilt. Behind the left company, on foot, a few armed retainers with swords at the belt. Between the horses, women who were dancing in a ring are breaking away, one still holding flowers; flowers on the paving. Spectators of the popolo (merchants, boys, old men, mothers with children) crowd the edges. At the far right edge, half in the crowd, Lapo, a lean dark-haired boy of sixteen in a plain tunic, and Gherardo, a slightly older youth in a neater clerk's gown, stand side by side, watching. No blood, no wound, no close-up of faces. Ink outline and restrained watercolour wash, matching the course's earlier scenes. No text, lettering, numbers or captions anywhere.

words_with_history.title: Dal latino all'italiano
words_with_history.text: «Ho fatto un errore», disse Lapo. «Chi l'ha detto?» «Avete scritto il conto dei fanti?» «Gli hanno tagliato il naso!»
words_with_history.note_en:
Italian builds its compound past from avere + participle, a pattern already forming in late Latin: habeo litteras scriptas, "I have the letters written", came to mean "I have written the letters". So habeo factum gives ho fatto ("I have done"), the pattern of every passato prossimo with avere. The Latin perfect itself lives on as the remoto: fecit → fece.

Many participles continue the Latin ones, with the consonant group made a double consonant: ct → tt in factum → fatto, dictum → detto; pt → tt in scriptum → scritto, ruptum → rotto ("broken"). These are correspondences to recognise, not a rule to apply: visto is a later remodelling (reconstructed *vistum), not classical visum, and shows no ct or pt; preso, messo and chiuso continue prensum, missum and clusum (a variant of clausum).

The pronoun gli comes from illi, the dative of ille, as the article il comes from illum: a Latin dative still used as a dative, "to him".

Words of the brawl: naso is nasus. Spada is spatha, a broad blade, the long cavalry sword of the late Roman army. Ferire is Latin ferire, "strike", narrowed to "wound": hanno ferito un Cerchi, they have wounded a Cerchi.

Senses that moved: donna is domina, "mistress, lady", now the ordinary word for "woman" (Latin femina); gente is gentem, in Latin a clan or nation, now any "people"; cavallo is caballus, in classical Latin a work horse or nag; the noble word equus left no everyday Italian descendant, and cavaliere (caballarius) is now a knight. Fermare is firmare, "make firm", hence "make stand still, stop". Piangere is plangere, "beat the breast, lament", which already shaded into weeping; in Italian it is the ordinary word for "weep" (Latin flere).

grammar.note_en:
**Passato prossimo: the tense of news.** The narrator tells May Day in the passato remoto, as in every chapter: Una spada passò davanti alla sua faccia e gli tagliò il naso (A sword passed in front of his face and cut off his nose). In the streets the same event arrives as news, in a compound tense, the passato prossimo: «Hanno ferito un Cerchi!» (They've wounded a Cerchi!), «Gli hanno tagliato il naso!» (They've cut his nose off!). The table Vide e ha visto sets the two side by side: Una spada gli tagliò il naso against «Gli hanno tagliato il naso!»; Le donne fuggirono (the women fled) against «le donne sono fuggite in chiesa» (the women have fled into the church).

**Which past, when.** In this dialogue the passato prossimo presents completed events as fresh news, or as still relevant to the speaker's present: what happened this morning or an hour ago, or anything whose result is still in front of the speaker. Bindo's «Questa mattina abbiamo venduto due panni» (This morning we sold two cloths) is a passato prossimo for that reason, and English often translates it with a simple past, as here. For a day before today a Tuscan speaker can still use the remoto (ieri lo vidi, I saw him yesterday: chapter 3), and narration uses it throughout. This is a tendency, not a calendar rule: how close the event feels and whether it still matters count as much as the day. Much of modern Italy, the north above all, has largely replaced the remoto with the prossimo for completed events in speech (the imperfect stays); this course keeps the Tuscan habit in dialogue.

**How it is built.** The present of avere or essere + the past participle. Latin had no such active tense, but late Latin habeo litteras scriptas, "I have the letters written", slid into "I have written the letters" (Dal latino, below). Most verbs take avere: ho visto (I have seen), hai visto (have you seen?), ha chiuso (has closed), abbiamo venduto (we have sold), avete sentito (have you heard?), hanno ferito (they have wounded). Several common verbs of movement or change take essere instead; here venire, cadere, uscire, fuggire, andare and tornare. Learn each verb with its auxiliary: sei venuto (you have come), è caduto (has fallen), è uscito (has gone out), è andato ... non è ancora tornato (has gone ... has not yet come back). With essere the participle agrees with the subject like an adjective, as the Latin perfect of a deponent does (profecti sunt, they have set out): i Donati sono fuggiti (the Donati have fled), le donne sono fuggite (the women have fled), tre fiorini sono usciti (three florins have gone out). Essere itself takes essere: «Chi è stato?» (Who did it?, literally "who has been?"); «È stata una bella festa» (It has been a fine festival), stata agreeing with festa.

**Participles.** Regular verbs: -are → -ato (tagliare, tagliato; contare, contato), -ere → -uto (vendere, venduto), -ire → -ito (ferire, ferito; sentire, sentito; uscire, uscito). Many common verbs have a strong participle that continues the Latin one: fatto (factum), detto (dictum), scritto (scriptum), preso, messo, chiuso, aperto (apertum); and the adjective morto (mortuus). Vedere has two, visto and veduto; Bindo, an old man, says «Ne ho veduti venti» (I saw twenty of them). Dal latino, below, shows the sound changes. A participle can also stand alone as an adjective: il libro grande, aperto (the big book, open); «È scritto, messere» (it is written, sir).

**After a pronoun, agreement with avere too.** With avere the participle normally keeps -o: hanno ferito un Cerchi, ho visto il sangue. When a direct-object lo, la, li or le stands before it, it agrees with that pronoun (with mi, ti, ci, vi agreement is optional; the indirect gli and le never cause it): «Quelli là li ho visti dagli Spini» (Those ones, I've seen them at the Spini's); «li abbiamo venduti noi» (we sold them ourselves). With ne the participle agrees with what ne stands for: «Ne ho veduti venti» (I saw twenty of them, the fanti). Read this; the exercises do not ask for it.

**Gli, le, ne.** Gli and le are the indirect-object pronouns, the dative: gli = a lui (to him), from Latin illi; le = a lei (to her). Italian puts the person affected in the dative, as Latin can: una spada gli tagliò il naso, "a sword cut the nose to him", that is, cut off his nose (the dative of disadvantage, dativus incommodi); un'altra le teneva la mano (another woman was holding her hand). Like lo and la (chapter 3) they stand right before the verb. Do not confuse the pronoun gli with the article gli (gli Spini): the pronoun goes with a verb, the article with a noun. Ne comes from Latin inde, "from there"; here it is partitive, "of it, of them": Ne venivano altri da tutte le strade (more of them were coming from every street); «Ne ho veduti venti» (I saw twenty of them). With a number and no noun, Italian needs ne.

**The tables in English.** Vide e ha visto: Una spada gli tagliò il naso (A sword cut off his nose) / «Gli hanno tagliato il naso!» (They've cut his nose off!); Le donne fuggirono (The women fled) / «Le donne sono fuggite in chiesa» (The women have fled into the church); Un cavallo cadde (A horse fell) / «Un cavaliere è caduto da cavallo» (A rider has fallen from his horse); Le botteghe chiusero presto (The shops closed early) / «Ser Bindo ha chiuso la bottega presto» (Ser Bindo has closed the shop early). In avere + participio: ho visto, contato, fatto (I have seen, counted, made); hai visto (you have seen); ha chiuso, chiamato, dato (has closed, called, given: Ser Bindo, messer Vieri, or chi, "who"); abbiamo venduto (we have sold); avete sentito, scritto (you have heard, written); hanno ferito, tagliato, messo, preso, detto (they have wounded, cut, put, taken, said). In essere + participio: sei venuto (you have come); è stato, caduto, uscito (has been, fallen, gone out); è stata (it, la festa, has been); sono fuggiti, fuggite (have fled: masculine, feminine); sono usciti (have gone out). Gli, le, ne: gli = a lui (to him), le = a lei (to her), ne = di loro (of them); «Ne ho veduti venti» (I saw twenty of them).

**Read only.** Dimmi (tell me) is di' + mi, an imperative with the pronoun attached; imperatives are chapter 7's. Bellissima is bella + -issima (Latin -issima), "very beautiful". C'era, c'erano: there was, there were.

**Fact and fiction.** The clash at Santa Trinita on the evening of 1 May 1300, during the women's dancing, between companies of young riders of the two houses, and the loss of Ricoverino de' Cerchi's nose, are told by both Dino Compagni (Cronica I.22) and Giovanni Villani (Cronica VIII.39). They differ on how it started: Compagni says the Donati company set out to attack; Villani has the trouble grow out of the dance and the press of horses. This chapter names no attacker. Lapo, Gherardo, Baldo, Ser Bindo, the Cerchi kinsman, the twenty armed men and the entry that pays them are fiction.

A.title: A
A.instruction: The narrator tells May Day in the passato remoto; in the street people tell it as news, in the passato prossimo. Block 1: write the participle after avere. Block 2: write the participle after essere, agreeing with the subject. Block 3: write the pronoun that stands for a lui or a lei.

obrazec.prompt: Ser Bindo chiuse la bottega. → «Ser Bindo ha ___ la bottega.»

items.prompt: Una spada tagliò il naso a Ricoverino. → «Hanno ___ il naso a Ricoverino.» (tagliare)
items.explanation: tagliare → tagliato: -are verbs make the participle in -ato.

items.prompt: Lapo vide le spade alte sopra i cavalli. → «Ho ___ le spade alte sopra i cavalli.» (vedere)
items.explanation: vedere → visto (or the older veduto, Bindo's form).

obrazec.prompt: Le donne fuggirono. → «Le donne sono ___ in chiesa.»

items.prompt: I Donati fuggirono nelle loro case. → «I Donati sono ___ nelle loro case.»
items.explanation: With essere the participle agrees with the subject: i Donati, masculine plural → fuggiti.

obrazec.prompt: Una spada tagliò il naso a Ricoverino. → Una spada ___ tagliò il naso.

items.prompt: Un'altra donna teneva la mano alla madre del ragazzo. → Un'altra donna ___ teneva la mano.
items.explanation: a lei → le, before the verb.

B.instruction: Complete each sentence with a word from the bank, unchanged. Four words are not used.

I giovani dei Cerchi entrarono nella piazza a cavallo, tutti insieme: erano una ___.

C.title: C
C.instruction: Questions 1–2: answer in Italian or English, in your own words, then compare with the model. Questions 3–4, Dal latino all'italiano, in English or Italian: (3) write the Italian participles from the story that continue Latin factum, dictum and scriptum, in that order; (4) in «Gli hanno tagliato il naso!», which word continues Latin illi, and what does it mean here?

items.prompt: Chi c'era tra i fanti dei Donati, e che cosa faceva?
model_answers: C'era Baldo, il marito della sorella di Lapo: aveva la mano sulla spada, guardava l'altra parte della piazza e aspettava. Poi corse con i fanti dietro i cavalli dei Donati.
items.rubric: Lapo saw his brother-in-law Baldo on foot among the Donati's armed servants, hand on his sword, watching the side of the square the Cerchi would come from, as if waiting; in the fight he ran with the Donati fanti, sword in hand. Lapo told Gherardo nothing. An English answer is fine.

items.prompt: Perché Ser Bindo fece scrivere il conto dei fanti nel libro della compagnia?
model_answers: Perché tre fiorini sono usciti dalla compagnia, e dunque vanno nel libro. Per Ser Bindo il libro va avanti, anche quella notte.
items.rubric: Bindo treats the hired men as a payment like any other: the florins left the company, so the entry goes in the book (Tre fiorini sono usciti dalla compagnia. Dunque vanno nel libro). He keeps the book going on the night of the brawl, and when Lapo asks who pays, the Cerchi or the company, he says that tonight it is the same thing: the firm's books now record the family's quarrel. An English answer is fine.

fatto («Ho fatto un errore»), detto («L'hanno detto i fanti dei Cerchi»), scritto («Avete scritto il conto dei fanti?»). Latin ct and pt became a double tt: factum → fatto, dictum → detto, scriptum → scritto (and ruptum → rotto).

model_answers: Gli: vuole dire «a lui», a Ricoverino.
items.rubric: Gli continues illi, the dative of ille, and is still a dative: the indirect object, the person affected (Latin ei nasum praeciderunt, 'they cut his nose off', literally 'cut the nose to him'). Like lo and la it stands before the verb. The article gli (gli Spini) has the same form but comes before a noun.

vocabulary.current_sense: in front (davanti a: in front of, before)

provenance.author: Claude Opus 5.5
notes: Chapter 4 of design v4, written by Claude Opus 5.5 from plan/cards/ch04.md in the parallel wave (chapters 2–7 written at the same time; chapters 2–3 treated as written from their plan rows and cards). Draft; no audio; pictures planned only, none generated.

Story choices inside the card's beats: the clash is in the evening (Compagni I.22 'una sera'; chapter 15's frame 'la sera del primo maggio'; chapter 13's 'un'altra notte ... di maggio'). Gherardo says the Donati riders' names one by one and Lapo hears them all, so that chapter 5 can have Lapo give names everyone knows and leave out Baldo. Baldo is seen on foot among the Donati fanti, hand on his sword, waiting, then running with them sword in hand; he is never shown striking, and the text does not say whether he saw Lapo. No attacker is named (card History). Bindo already knows the news («Lo so») and saw the twenty fanti at messer Vieri's door himself («Li ho veduti»), leaving room for chapter 5's 'he saw Baldo too'. The Cerchi kinsman is unnamed, speaker char-cerchi-kinsman as continuity.json asks; he was one of the Cerchi riders.

Lexemes: 45 new, within the ceiling of 90: the 40 planned plus five writer additions used at least three times in the prose: piede (a piedi), fiore, spingere, tremare, avanti. Opaque by the plan's split: ballare, tagliare, gridare, fante, brigata, davanti, dietro, colpo, compagno, plus avanti and spingere (11, within 26).

Held model deltas: chapter 8 (davanti, fermare, passare, aprire, chiudere, tagliare) and chapter 15 (alto, colpo, compagno, forte, gettare, maggio, piangere, dietro, ferire, tagliare, cadere, chiudere, arma, aprire, correre) already date these entries to it-dante-01-l04 and carry no base card stages, so no held file was edited. Senses are copied with the same ids; alto and forte gain new sense ids it-alto-2 and it-forte-2 for 'loud(ly)' (a voce alta, gridò forte), which the held senses do not cover.

Forms of chapter 1–3 lexemes first used here (trovò, conosceva, aspettava, sentito, venduto, dati, tornato, siedi, dimmi …) are declared in this delta under their lexeme ids, entry first_lesson = the lexeme's plan chapter, form first_lesson = it-dante-01-l04. Chapters 2 and 3 are being written in parallel; on integration, where they declare the same form, the lower chapter's date wins.

New Latin bridge strings appended to course.json bridge_references.la under the COURSE.md rule: Kalendae Maiae, saltare, flores, iactare, pedes, pellere, flere, secare, ictus, tremere, dic mihi, equus, homines, porro, feminae. All are real Latin with the sense used. Ballare is glossed saltare (Latin 'dance'); reveal_en warns that Italian saltare means 'jump'. The card suggested an Italian definition (muovere i piedi con la musica), which would need muovere and piedi before they are known.

Donne is glossed feminae and gente homines (same sense) after the reviews, not the plan's domina and gentem, whose senses shifted (COURSE.md); avanti is glossed porro. Glossed single uses, not lexemes: Calendimaggio (Kalendae Maiae) and villani (rusticus, as in chapter 1).

Length: 1,305 running words against the advisory window of 1,350–1,850. Every card beat is staged; the critique rounds added only lines that carry plot (Gherardo naming the riders; the mother whose son has not come home). Further length would be padding (RULES §10).

Imperatives are short fixed commands, receptive only: Guarda, Siedi, Scrivi, Aprite, Vieni avanti (G01's fixed-command licence) and Dimmi (G04's receptive list). Siedi, Scrivi and Aprite have the same form as the present.

History (card; docs/it-dante-research.md): evening of 1 May 1300, women dancing at Santa Trinita, companies of young riders of both houses, horses pushed together, swords, Ricoverino de' Cerchi's nose cut off (Compagni I.22; Villani VIII.39). The brawl's start is told neutrally (both companies push their horses together): Compagni has the Donati attack, Villani the press of riders at the dance. Fiction: Lapo, Gherardo, Baldo, Bindo, the kinsman, the twenty fanti hired for the night and the three-florin entry. The sum is invented: about six or seven soldi a man for the night at roughly 45 soldi to the florin (research note: 40–50), not sourced.

Tap glosses: 56 forms appended to glosses/forms.json; glosses/capitolo-04.json gives occurrence senses where the dictionary default misfits (panni as cloth or as clothes; le = to her; mettere mano alla spada; chi è stato?; a voce alta).

review_questions.quote: È stata una bella festa, per i nobili
review_questions.question: [?] The old man's sarcasm: is «È stata una bella festa, per i nobili» idiomatic as bitter irony, said as he shuts his door?
review_questions.resolution: Codex review: idiomatic bitter irony; the closed door supplies the gesture, not a moral. Kept.

review_questions.quote: Il giovane gettò la spada sulla tavola
review_questions.question: [?] The kinsman throws his sword on the table beside the book before questioning Lapo: plausible as a young noble's pressure, or too theatrical?
review_questions.resolution: Codex review: forceful but acceptable fiction for the pressure scene. Kept.

review_questions.question: [?] The grammar note gives the Tuscan use of the passato prossimo for fresh or still-relevant events and keeps the remoto for narration. Is the claim cautious enough?
review_questions.resolution: Sol and Codex: acceptable with the caveat. The note now leads with fresh news and present relevance, calls the day boundary a tendency, not a rule, and makes no claim about exact spoken usage in 1300.

review_questions.quote: dati per i fanti di questa notte
review_questions.question: [?] The account-book formula «dati per i fanti di questa notte ... tre fiorini d'oro» imitates chapter 13's «Dati a Tano Baldovini …». Is the sum (three florins for twenty men for a night) plausible? It is invented and disclosed.
review_questions.resolution: Codex review: not verified; it would need a dated comparable payment. Non-blocking while the payment stays disclosed as fiction (grammar note, provenance).

review_questions.question: [?] Latin margin glosses against the plan row: the plan's first_use_aids give donne ⟦domina⟧, gente ⟦gentem⟧ and ferito ⟦ferire⟧.
review_questions.resolution: Following Sol (twice), Codex and the fresh-eyes review, donne is now ⟦feminae⟧ and gente ⟦homines⟧, same-sense Latin; domina → donna and gentem → gente move to Dal latino (COURSE.md: shifted etymons go there). Ferito keeps the card's ⟦ferire⟧, whose strike → wound narrowing reveal_en and Dal latino state; reviewers accepted it.
